items.q: Which line shows the equation for photosynthesis written in chemical symbols?
items.correct: CO2 and H2O react to form C6H12O6 and O2.
items.misconception: C6H12O6 and O2 form CO2 and H2O.
items.why: The two equations look like mirror images of each other, so reactants and products get swapped. Being told that plants 'give out oxygen' is also heard as 'plants do not use oxygen', and the site of each reaction is mixed up. Photosynthesis is represented by: carbon dioxide + water → (light) glucose + oxygen, and it takes place in the chloroplasts. The glucose produced in photosynthesis may be used for respiration, so plants carry out both reactions.
items.random_wrong: CO2 and O2 produce C6H12O6 and H2O.

items.q: Which statement describes photosynthesis as an endothermic reaction?
items.correct: Energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts by light.
items.misconception: Energy is transferred from the chloroplasts to the environment.
items.why: Students meet glucose as the energy store used in respiration, so they assume that any reaction which produces glucose must release energy. The word 'light' written over the arrow is also read as a product of the reaction rather than as the energy that is taken in. Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction: energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts by light. Energy is taken in by the reaction, it is not given out.
items.random_wrong: Energy is transferred from the surroundings to the mitochondria.

items.q: A student measures the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed by counting bubbles of oxygen. She counts 90 bubbles in 3 minutes. What is the rate of photosynthesis?
items.why: Students record the largest number in their results table and read it as 'how much photosynthesis happened'. Rate is not yet treated as a quantity measured per unit of time, so the time column is ignored or is multiplied in rather than divided by. Rate of photosynthesis is calculated as the amount of product formed divided by the time taken, for example bubbles of oxygen per minute or cm3 of oxygen per minute.

items.q: A student plots the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed against light intensity at a constant temperature. The graph rises steeply and then becomes a horizontal line. Which statement explains the horizontal part of the graph?
items.correct: Another factor, such as temperature, is now limiting the rate.
items.misconception: Light intensity is still limiting the rate on the flat part.
items.why: Light is taught as the thing that drives photosynthesis, so students treat it as the only factor that matters and look for damage to the plant or a fault in the experiment to explain a flat line, instead of using the idea of a limiting factor. Light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis, but the factors interact and any one of them may be the factor that limits photosynthesis. Where the graph is flat, a factor other than light intensity is limiting the rate.
items.random_wrong: The plant has switched from photosynthesis to respiration.

items.q: A graph shows the rate of photosynthesis against light intensity at 20 °C and at 30 °C, both at the same carbon dioxide concentration. Both curves rise and then become horizontal, but the 30 °C curve becomes horizontal at a higher rate. Which statement about the graph is correct?
items.correct: Temperature is limiting the rate where the 20 °C curve is flat.
items.misconception: Light intensity limits the rate where the 20 °C curve is flat.
items.why: Light is taught as the thing that drives photosynthesis, so students treat it as the only factor that matters and look for damage to the plant or a fault in the experiment to explain a flat line, instead of using the idea of a limiting factor. Light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis, but the factors interact and any one of them may be the factor that limits photosynthesis. Where the graph is flat, a factor other than light intensity is limiting the rate.
items.random_wrong: Temperature is limiting the rate on the steep part of every curve.

items.q: A lamp is moved from 10 cm to 20 cm from a piece of pondweed. Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the lamp. What happens to the light intensity reaching the pondweed?
items.correct: It falls to 1/4 of the light intensity at 10 cm.
items.misconception: It falls to 1/2 of the intensity at 10 cm.
items.why: Inverse proportion is normally met as y being proportional to 1/x, so students apply simple inverse proportion to the distance and do not square it. Distances in centimetres are also used directly in the fraction instead of the change in distance. Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source. Doubling the distance reduces the light intensity to 1/2 squared, which is one quarter.
items.random_wrong: It falls to 1/10 of the intensity at 10 cm.

items.q: How does a plant obtain the amino acids it uses for protein synthesis?
items.correct: Amino acids are made from glucose and nitrate ions.
items.misconception: Amino acids are made from starch and nitrate ions.
items.why: The iodine test for starch is used in class to show that a leaf has photosynthesised, so students conclude that starch is the direct product of the reaction and stop distinguishing it from the glucose in the equation. The equation shows that photosynthesis produces glucose (C6H12O6). The glucose produced may then be used for respiration, converted into insoluble starch for storage, used to produce fat or oil for storage, used to produce cellulose, or used to produce amino acids.
items.random_wrong: Amino acids are absorbed from the soil by the roots.

items.q: A water plant is given bright light and kept at a warm temperature, but the water around it contains very little carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide concentration in the water is then slowly increased. Which statement describes what happens to the rate of photosynthesis?
items.correct: It increases, then levels off once another factor becomes limiting.
items.misconception: It stays the same, because the plant makes its own carbon dioxide.
items.why: Students know that plants respire and release carbon dioxide, so they assume a plant supplies its own carbon dioxide for photosynthesis and that the surrounding concentration is unimportant. Carbon dioxide from the air, or dissolved in water, is a raw material for photosynthesis. Its concentration is a limiting factor, which is why growers add carbon dioxide in greenhouses to raise the rate.
items.random_wrong: It falls, because carbon dioxide is a harmful waste gas for the plant.

items.q: A variegated leaf is green in some areas, which contain chlorophyll, and white in others, which contain none. After the leaf has been left in bright light, in which areas has photosynthesis taken place?
items.correct: In the green areas only, because chlorophyll is needed to absorb light for photosynthesis.
items.misconception: In the white areas, once the green areas have used up their chlorophyll.
items.why: Students see chlorophyll listed as needed for photosynthesis and treat it like carbon dioxide or water, which are used up, instead of as a pigment that absorbs light without being consumed. Chlorophyll is not a reactant and does not appear in the equation. It absorbs light for the reaction but is not used up, so the amount of chlorophyll stays available to affect the rate.
items.random_wrong: In the white areas as well, because every part of a leaf photosynthesises.

items.q: A greenhouse grower can raise the light intensity, temperature and carbon dioxide concentration to speed up photosynthesis and increase the crop yield, but each of these costs money. Which statement best describes how far the grower should raise a factor?
items.correct: Raise a factor only while the extra crop it gives is worth more than the extra cost.
items.misconception: Set the light, temperature and carbon dioxide as high as the greenhouse can go.
items.why: Students learn that raising light intensity, temperature and carbon dioxide concentration speeds up photosynthesis, so they assume the aim is always the fastest possible rate. They overlook that enhancing each condition costs money and that the purpose of a commercial greenhouse is profit, not the maximum rate. Limiting factors are important in the economics of a greenhouse. It is worth raising a factor only while the extra crop it produces is worth more than the extra cost of raising it, and no further once another factor has become the limiting factor.
items.random_wrong: Keep on adding carbon dioxide even after light intensity has become the limiting factor.

items.q: A young tree is planted in a tub of soil and watered regularly. Over several years it grows and gains a large mass of wood, leaves and roots. Where does most of this extra mass mainly come from?
items.correct: Mostly from carbon dioxide taken in from the air and used in photosynthesis.
items.misconception: Mostly from minerals in the soil, taken up through the roots.
items.why: Plants are rooted in soil and have to be watered, so students picture the plant building its body from material drawn out of the ground. It seems impossible that so much solid mass could come from an invisible gas in the air. The carbon in a plant's glucose, and in the starch and cellulose made from it, comes from carbon dioxide fixed from the air in photosynthesis. Water is a raw material too, but the soil supplies only small amounts of mineral ions, not the bulk of the mass.
items.random_wrong: Mostly from the water it is given, taken up through the roots.

items.q: Does raising the temperature always increase the rate of photosynthesis?
items.correct: Raising the temperature increases the rate only while temperature is the limiting factor; at high temperatures the enzymes controlling photosynthesis are denatured and the rate falls.
items.misconception: The warmer a plant is kept, the faster it photosynthesises, so raising the temperature increases the rate whatever the starting temperature is.
items.why: Students generalise from the rising part of a rate-temperature graph, and from the rule met in chemistry that heating makes reactions go faster. They forget that photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes, which are denatured at high temperatures. Temperature affects the rate of photosynthesis. It increases the rate while it is the limiting factor, but above the optimum temperature the enzymes are denatured and the rate falls.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where do the proteins in a plant come from?
items.correct: The plant makes them: glucose produced in photosynthesis is used with nitrate ions absorbed from the soil to produce amino acids for protein synthesis.
items.misconception: Plants take in ready-made protein from the soil through their roots, which is why fertiliser has to be added to the soil.
items.why: Fertiliser is described as 'plant food', so students picture the soil as supplying finished food substances such as protein, rather than ions that the plant uses to build molecules for itself. To produce proteins, plants use nitrate ions that are absorbed from the soil. These are used with the glucose produced in photosynthesis to produce amino acids for protein synthesis.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A plant has plenty of light and warmth but very little carbon dioxide. What happens to the rate of photosynthesis as the carbon dioxide concentration is raised?
items.correct: The rate increases while carbon dioxide is the limiting factor, then levels off once another factor, such as light intensity or temperature, becomes limiting.
items.misconception: The more carbon dioxide a plant is given, the faster it photosynthesises, so raising the carbon dioxide concentration increases the rate without limit.
items.why: Students learn that carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis and generalise from the rising part of a rate graph, forgetting that the factors interact and that another factor takes over as the limiting factor. Carbon dioxide concentration affects the rate while it is the limiting factor. Once it is no longer limiting, another factor limits the rate and increasing carbon dioxide further has no effect.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happens to the rate of photosynthesis when the carbon dioxide concentration is increased from a low level?
items.correct: The rate increases, because carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis and was limiting the rate.
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide is a harmful waste gas, so increasing its concentration around a plant lowers the rate of photosynthesis.
items.why: Students meet carbon dioxide as a waste product of respiration and as a pollutant linked to global warming, so they treat it as harmful to the plant rather than as a reactant the plant needs. Carbon dioxide is a reactant in photosynthesis. When it is the limiting factor, increasing its concentration increases the rate of photosynthesis, it does not decrease it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A variegated leaf has green areas that contain chlorophyll and white areas that contain none. In which areas can photosynthesis take place?
items.correct: Only in the green areas, because chlorophyll is needed to absorb light for photosynthesis.
items.misconception: Every part of a leaf photosynthesises, so the white areas of a variegated leaf photosynthesise just like the green areas.
items.why: Students are taught that leaves are the organs of photosynthesis, so they assume the whole leaf photosynthesises and overlook that the white areas contain no chlorophyll to absorb light. The amount of chlorophyll affects the rate of photosynthesis. The white areas contain no chlorophyll, so they cannot absorb light and do not photosynthesise; only the green areas do.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A magnesium-deficient plant makes less chlorophyll and its leaves turn pale. What effect does this have on the rate of photosynthesis?
items.correct: The rate falls, because there is less chlorophyll to absorb light for photosynthesis.
items.misconception: Chlorophyll only gives a leaf its green colour, so the amount of chlorophyll does not affect the rate of photosynthesis.
items.why: Chlorophyll is first met as the pigment that makes plants green, so students think its only job is colour and do not connect the amount of chlorophyll with how much light can be absorbed for photosynthesis. Chlorophyll absorbs the light used in photosynthesis, so the amount of chlorophyll is a factor that affects the rate. Less chlorophyll means less light absorbed and a lower rate.
